periodos.nombre: Middle Bronze Age — One of the Plain Cities destroyed

descripcion_geo: One of the five 'Cities of the Plain' (along with Sodom, Gomorrah, Zeboim and Zoar) located in the region of the southern Jordan Valley or in the basin of the Salt Sea, destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah according to the Genesis account.
clima: Extreme desert — typical of the Salt Sea region, with very little precipitation and high temperatures.
recursos: Position on the fertile southern Jordan plain before the destruction (described as 'like the garden of YHWH')
importancia_estrategica: Adma is part of the group of cities destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah, and its name becomes a recurring prophetic reference as a paradigmatic example of the harshest possible divine judgment, cited in later oracles against other nations as a comparative measure of definitive destruction.

otros_habitantes.descripcion: Local king of Adma, member of the coalition of five kings of the Plain Cities initially defeated by Chedorlaomer and his allies.
Inhabitants of the city, destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah by the divine judgment narrated in Genesis 19.

historias.titulo: Sinab, king of Adma, in the war of the five kings
historias.descripcion: Sinab, king of Adma, is part of the coalition of five kings of the Cities of the Plain who rebels against Chedorlaomer and is defeated in the valley of Siddim, an episode that precedes the capture of Lot, resident in Sodom.

historias.titulo: Adma destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah
historias.descripcion: Adma is mentioned along with Sodom, Gomorrah, and Zeboim as cities destroyed by divine fire and brimstone, in contrast to Zoar, which is spared at Lot's request to serve as an immediate refuge.

historias.titulo: Hosea invokes the memory of Adma as a warning and promise
historias.descripcion: The prophet Hosea uses the memory of the destruction of Adma and Zeboim in an oracle where YHWH expresses his compassion towards Israel, promising that his heart is moved and he will not treat Ephraim as he treated those cities, despite the justice that such punishment would deserve.

personajes.rol: King of Adma, member of the Plains Cities coalition
personajes.descripcion: Ruler of Adma defeated along with his allies by Chedorlaomer, an episode that precedes the definitive destruction of his city along with Sodom and Gomorrah.

personajes.rol: Resident of the Plain Cities region
personajes.descripcion: Although he resides specifically in Sodom, his choice to settle on the fertile Jordan plain links him directly to the fate of neighboring cities, including Adma, at the time of destruction.
He invokes the memory of Adma as a compassionate contrast: unlike that irrevocably destroyed city, YHWH expresses his desire not to treat Israel in the same definitive way despite his infidelity.

contexto_religioso.contexto_lugar: Adma is part of the set of Cities of the Plain whose destruction becomes a recurring paradigmatic reference throughout the entire subsequent biblical corpus to illustrate both the severity of divine judgment and, paradoxically, also its compassionate contrast in passages such as the oracle of Hosea, where the very memory of the destruction of Adma serves to highlight the mercy that YHWH chooses to exercise towards Israel despite deserving a similar fate.

mitos.nombre: Adma and Zeboim as a comparative reference of divine judgment

judaismo.fuente_secundaria: Comentario rabínico tradicional sobre el uso de Adma y Zeboim como medida estándar de comparación para el juicio divino más severo en oráculos posteriores
judaismo.descripcion: Jewish tradition observes that Adma and Zeboim, although less prominent individually than Sodom and Gomorrah, function in the later biblical text as a unit of rhetorical measurement to express the magnitude of devastating judgment, and that their mention in Hosea as a foil for divine compassion toward Israel reveals a fundamental theological tension between deserved justice and chosen mercy.
judaismo.significado_teologico: The contrast between Adma's irrevocable destruction and the compassion promised to Israel illustrates the central tension of prophetic theology between retributive justice and YHWH's elective mercy.
